39: This plan describes a wedding and event venue on a leased rural or semi-rural property with existing buildings: a barn or farmhouse, a garden, a hall that seats {{aforo}} guests and, as a rain plan, a pergola and a tent, plus a bridal suite, ADA-compliant restrooms, a gravel parking lot and a prep and warming kitchen for the caterer. You do not buy the property, you lease it, and the food and drinks come from an exclusive caterer who pays you a commission. You sell the venue rental fee and the event services, which make up {{espacio_pct}} of sales ({{ventas_espacio_a1}} in year 1). The caterer bills the menu and the bar directly to the couple, serves alcohol under its own license, and pays you a caterer commission (10% of its food and beverage sales at the venue, an assumption you negotiate) that makes up {{comision_caterer_pct}} of your sales: {{comision_caterer_a1}} in year 1. Interest is real: DataForSEO shows roughly 1,000 monthly US searches for "wedding venue business plan" and 720 for "event venue business plan". One warning up front: zoning approval, the conditional use permit and the certificate of occupancy decide whether there is a business at all, so check with your county before you spend anything.
40: The key figures of the example case are these. We run {{dias}} events a year across weddings, corporate events, private celebrations and micro weddings, with {{clientes_dia}} guests per event on average and {{ticket}} of revenue per guest to the venue excl. sales tax ({{precio_menu}} incl. sales tax). That gives year-1 revenue of {{ventas_a1}} and a net profit of {{resultado_neto_a1}}, a net margin of {{margen_neto_a1}}. Accounting break-even is {{equilibrio_eventos}} events a year of the average size, and cash break-even, which also covers the loan payments, is {{equilibrio_caja_eventos}}. This is not a guaranteed return: it is a starting point so you can change the assumptions and enter your own numbers, from your county, your market and your caterer.
41: Total investment is {{inversion_total}}: {{capex}} of startup costs (permits and drawings, renovation, restrooms, fire safety, ceremony site, parking, sound and launch, plus a {{inv_fianza}} lease security deposit, {{inv_renta_previa}} of rent paid during permitting and a {{inv_imprevistos}} build-out contingency) and {{fondo_maniobra}} of working capital. The cash needed at opening is {{necesidad_caja}}. It is financed with {{fondos_propios}} of owner's equity ({{aportacion_pct}} of the cash needed) and a {{prestamo}} loan over {{plazo_prestamo}} years at {{tipo_prestamo}} (nominal, not APR), for example an SBA 7(a) loan through your lender: lender-ready, approval not guaranteed. The annual loan payment is {{cuota_anual}}. Because the build-out sits on land you do not own, SBA lenders typically require a lease whose term, counting extension options, is at least as long as the loan; confirm with your lender.
42: Year 1 counts the full {{dias}} events, which is only possible if the first season is sold during permitting through holds contingent on the CUP and the certificate of occupancy, which become firm when you get them; if not, look at the pessimistic scenario in the Excel. Revenue is {{ventas_a1}} and net profit {{resultado_neto_a1}}, or {{margen_neto_a1}} of sales. Growth in years 2 and 3 is counted in equivalent events at the same revenue per guest: {{eventos_equivalentes_a2}} and {{eventos_equivalentes_a3}}. Revenue rises to {{ventas_a2}} and {{ventas_a3}}, and net profit to {{resultado_neto_a2}} and {{resultado_neto_a3}}, with net margins of {{margen_neto_a2}} and {{margen_neto_a3}}. The margin of safety over cash break-even is {{holgura_caja_pct}} in year 1, {{holgura_caja_a2}} in year 2 and {{holgura_caja_a3}} in year 3, and the lowest DSCR over the loan term is {{dscr_min}}. Payback before debt: {{payback}}.
43: The team is small and leans on you. You run the venue, sell the dates, give the tours and coordinate every event, supported by a small team ({{plantilla_puestos}} people including you, {{plantilla_jornadas}} full-time equivalents, with the venue coordinator and the event attendants as seasonal W-2 employees) who handle setup, cleaning and parking. There are no servers or kitchen staff on your payroll: the exclusive caterer provides them and is also responsible for the food safety of the menu. The kit includes this ten-section business plan, the nine-tab Excel financial plan, the 84-task startup checklist in six phases, the venue pricing calculator, the contract templates (a venue rental agreement for couples and private events with a corporate addendum, and the exclusive caterer agreement; templates, not legal advice) and the Equivalents Guide.
46: There are three common ways to run a wedding venue, and you should choose before you sign anything. In the first, the venue has in-house catering: it cooks and serves the banquet, and that is a different business, with a production kitchen, a food cost to manage and a much larger payroll, built for people from the restaurant world; if that is you, look at the Catering Business Plan Kit. In the second, an exclusive caterer serves the menu and pays the venue a caterer commission, which is the model of this plan. In the third, the venue is rental only: the couple brings an outside caterer from a preferred vendor list or any licensed caterer, and you charge a venue rental fee and sometimes an outside catering fee. Each model has its own investment, permits and margin, and each is a real choice: a banquet hall in town or hiring a wedding planner to run the venue for you are other routes, but they are not what this kit models.
47: The plan picks the exclusive caterer for three reasons. You do not need a production kitchen, which costs far more than a prep and warming kitchen, nor a kitchen crew. The food safety of the menu belongs to the caterer, not to you. And rental only gives up the commission: without the {{comision_caterer_a1}} of year 1, the venue loses a real share of its margin, and you should test that in the pessimistic scenario of the Excel. Buying the property is a different investment: it usually costs far more up front than leasing (typical range, get local quotes), and financing it with an SBA 504 loan is a variant to discuss with your lender and your CPA; the Excel does not model it. The plan leases a property with existing buildings, or one from a relative at market rent, at {{alquiler_mes}} a month ({{ocupacion_pct}} of sales). Negotiate a long lease whose term, counting extension options, is at least as long as the loan (SBA lenders typically require this; confirm with your lender), a purchase option or right of first refusal, the owner's written consent to the build-out and to using the lease as collateral, a tenant improvement (TI) allowance, reduced rent during the build-out and a lease contingent on CUP approval.
48: What the venue sells is the space, the ceremony, the setup, the day-of coordination and the peace of mind of having a single caterer responsible for the food. The client pays the venue the venue rental fee and the services of the event, with the sales tax your state applies, and pays the caterer the menu and the bar. For you that means one point of contact with the caterer and, for the couple, a day without loose ends.
49: The day-to-day of an average event is measured with simple numbers. The venue team spends {{horas_evento}} hours on each event between setup, coordination, cleaning and parking, with {{personas_evento}} people on site at the same time, plus {{horas_estructura}} hours of off-day work per event for tours, planning and turnover. The venue earns {{ingreso_evento}} on an average event, with {{clientes_dia}} guests at {{ticket}} per guest excl. sales tax. All variable costs together take {{costes_variables_pct}} of sales. It matters to look at the whole event and not just the price: growth in years 2 and 3 comes from more activity at the same revenue per guest, not from raising your rates.
50: The concept does not end with the big wedding. The case mix has 35 weddings of 130 guests, 25 corporate events of 70, 30 private celebrations of 80 and 10 micro weddings of 30, always counted per guest and excl. sales tax. Weddings give the highest price, but companies and milestone birthdays, showers and anniversaries fill the calendar that weddings leave empty, above all on weekdays and in the off-season. With that mix the venue works most of the year and the seasonal team has work beyond the summer.
53: The wedding market in the United States is large, seasonal and well documented, but the numbers change every year: national wedding studies publish yearly averages, so check the latest before you quote one to a lender. What matters for a venue is the pattern. Weddings cluster in the fall, with September and October as peaks, and again in June, while January and February are the trough. A barn venue lives on a few dozen prime Saturdays, which is why the plan sells other days and other event types around them. Surveys of couples are also biased toward the big wedding, so treat any single national average with caution.
54: Couples usually book a wedding venue 12-18 months ahead (Kit estimate), ask several venues for information and tour a few, and most start online. That sets your calendar: dates are sold long before the event exists. Search demand is clear and it comes from clients, not only from entrepreneurs: DataForSEO shows roughly 6,600 monthly US searches for "wedding barn". Rates vary a lot by region, season and day of the week: published rate cards are a typical range, get local quotes, and treat them as advertised prices, not collected ones. The Excel and the pricing calculator give you the structure to set your own.
55: Weddings are only part of the business. Companies look for retreats, meetings, holiday parties and team building; families look for graduation parties, showers, anniversaries and milestone birthdays; and there are small events that nobody wants in a huge hall, such as micro weddings, elopements and rehearsal dinners. They all fill what weddings do not cover, on weekdays and in the off-season. That is why the case splits the {{dias}} events into four types and does not depend only on a June Saturday. When you work out the numbers, do not assume a market size nobody publishes: what counts is how many dates you can sell in your area, and you can check that with tours and bookings.
56: With Month 1 in March, the plan spreads sales with seasonality: the peak arrives with summer and early fall, and the trough with winter. The start has a 12-month ramp-up that begins well below full pace, because weddings are booked 12-18 months ahead. The lowest cash balance, {{saldo_minimo}}, comes in month {{mes_saldo_minimo}}, just after the investment is paid and before the bulk of the season arrives: that first spring is carried by the {{fondo_maniobra}} of working capital. After that, the season lifts the cash and carries you through the first winter, when rent and staff stay flat but few events are booked.
57: The gap is clear: much of what you find online is generic templates, or advice for couples planning their own wedding, and very little walks you through the business of a wedding venue with a live Excel model. This document draws on public US sources named in the text and on the kit's own estimates, which it labels as such.
58: Demand has risks that the plan names. A price war over Saturday dates pushes rates down, clients may want to bring their own caterer, and a rainy spring demands that the hall and the tent rain plan be ready. The biggest risk is occupancy: below {{equilibrio_caja_eventos}} events of the average size there is no cash in year 1, and from year 2, when you are repaying principal, the margin of safety over cash break-even is {{holgura_caja_a2}} and then {{holgura_caja_a3}}, so every date you do not sell shows.
61: Before you set any price, draw the map of who competes with you and who you sell to. Your clients are couples, with a large or an intimate wedding, companies, families celebrating graduations, showers and milestone birthdays, and the intermediaries who bring clients: wedding planners, event agencies and venue marketplaces, which bring {{intermediarios_pct}} of sales with a {{comision_intermediarios_pct}} commission. Each decides for different reasons, so analyze them separately.
62: What each client decides on is the first thing to understand. The couple looks at the date, the capacity, the setting, the catering, the price, lodging and the rain plan. The company looks at access, parking, connectivity and a day that does not get complicated. The family looks at the price and at having everything solved by one person. The wedding planner looks for a clear calendar, a commission that is paid on time and a space that can be set up without surprises. A venue wins if it answers all of that with a well-prepared tour and a quote that makes sense at first read. It loses if every extra feels like a new negotiation, or if the exclusive caterer feels like an imposition instead of an advantage. Note the venue price per guest ({{ticket}}) is what the venue bills: it is not what the couple pays for the whole wedding.
63: Competition comes from several sides, and you do not need brand names to see it. There are other barn venues with in-house catering, venues with an exclusive caterer, rental-only venues, hotels and restaurants with a ballroom, charming farms, wineries and historic estates, urban banquet halls, and unusual spaces such as gardens and mansions. Your answer is not to lower the price: it is a clear calendar with well-sold dates, one point of contact for the food, a visible venue rental fee, a rain plan with hall and tent, and weekday sales to companies.
64: The entry barriers are compliance and cash. Zoning approval decides whether there is a business: on rural land, hosting weddings is often not an ordinary use, and it typically requires a conditional (special) use permit and a certificate of occupancy for assembly use. The rules vary by county and state, so check with your county planning office, your building official and your fire marshal, and with your attorney. Do not confirm firm dates without them (before you have them, take only holds contingent on them, fully refundable if they never arrive), and make the lease contingent on CUP approval. Cash also weighs: the depreciable build-out in the case is {{base_obra}}, and furniture and equipment add {{base_equipo}}.
65: Four factors decide whether it works. The first is the calendar: how many dates of the first season you book, contingent on the permits, while you process them and do the build-out. The second is the space: a setting that looks good in photos, with a hall and a tent for the rain plan and enough parking. The third is the exclusive caterer: a reliable partner, with a negotiated caterer commission that is easy to audit. The fourth is cash control: cash break-even is {{equilibrio_caja_eventos}} events in year 1, with a margin of safety of {{holgura_caja_pct}}, and the margin changes to {{holgura_caja_a2}} and {{holgura_caja_a3}} in years 2 and 3 once you are repaying principal, so every date without a booking shows.
66: The SWOT of this concept is clear. Strengths: a model without your own kitchen or kitchen crew, one point of contact for the food and a gross margin of {{margen_bruto_pct}} in year 1. Weaknesses: a high investment, an uncertain permit and a strong dependence on the caterer. Opportunities: companies, graduations and milestone birthdays on weekdays, and selling to wedding planners and agencies. Threats: a price war on Saturday dates, the client who wants to bring an outside caterer, and rain. The defense is the calendar, the rain plan, the contract with the caterer and dates that are sold early.
69: Lead generation starts 12-18 months ahead, because that is how a wedding is planned. Being on The Knot and WeddingWire storefronts, with complete listings, is the first step; the second is bridal shows and open houses with the exclusive caterer and a tasting. In the case, bridal shows and open houses cost {{ferias_anual}} a year. The most important thing about the first season is this: dates are booked during the months of permitting and build-out, before opening, as holds contingent on the permits with a full refund agreed in writing if they do not arrive in time; once you have them, they become firm bookings with a retainer applied to the price. Never confirm a firm date without the permits. If you sign couples at bridal shows or off-site, ask your attorney whether the FTC Cooling-Off Rule or your state's home-solicitation law applies; many venues give a short cancellation window for show-floor signings anyway.
70: The venue tour is where the sale closes. Because the couple asks several venues for information and tours a few, prepare it like a small show: confirm the date they want, walk them from the ceremony site to the reception, have the rain plan ready with hall and tent, and present the menu with the exclusive caterer on the same visit. Leave with a clear quote, a date on hold with a deadline and a rental agreement. The client who leaves without knowing the price rarely comes back.
71: Wedding planners, event agencies and venue marketplaces such as Peerspace are a decisive channel: {{intermediarios_pct}} of sales comes through them, with a {{comision_intermediarios_pct}} commission. Treat them as partners. Show them the venue before anyone else, give them an up-to-date calendar with available dates, a written venue rental fee and quick answers. The commission is a cost of acquiring clients, not a discount, and the Excel includes it ({{comisiones_intermediarios_a1}} in year 1). The clearer the deal, the more dates they will bring. Check the commission in each marketplace contract.
72: The website is your permanent storefront. With an up-to-date availability calendar, a description of the spaces, photos and video of all four seasons, the event types, a pricing guide and a contact form, it does its job before the tour. Complete your Google Business Profile and your storefront listings, ask for reviews after each event and answer all of them, including the bad ones, kindly. Social media shows the venue in action: setups, ceremonies, the garden, the rain plan and details of the day. A venue management software such as Tripleseat, Perfect Venue or HoneyBook keeps leads, proposals and the calendar in one place.
73: Companies and private celebrations fill the gaps. Offer retreats, meetings, holiday parties and team building on weekdays, and graduation parties, showers and anniversaries outside the wedding season. To fill the slow months and the days with less demand, publish peak, shoulder and off-peak prices, with visible discounts for Fridays, Sundays and the winter months. A clear price and an honest calendar convince more than a last-minute offer, and they protect the value of the summer Saturday. The pricing calculator in this kit builds those tiers for you.
74: Loyalty is simple. A satisfied client recommends you, a company comes back every year, a family returns for the next milestone birthday. A venue lives on trust, and that trust is built after the lights go out. Keep in touch with an email after the event, a request for a review and a notice with the available dates for next season. We do not estimate conversion rates, because they depend on your market and how you work it: measure them yourself during the first season. The best marketing is a well-run event, a warm approach and a client who feels their day mattered.
75: The marketing budget of the case is {{marketing_anual}} a year for the storefronts, Google Ads and social media, plus {{ferias_anual}} for bridal shows and open houses and {{inv_lanzamiento}} for the launch within the initial investment. The first year starts working from day one, with the website and listings ready and the first season's dates on hold, contingent on the permits, before opening. If an action does not bring tours, correct it or change it, and move the money to the one that does.
